texts.161g-gA-fix9to11:
In 2023 the Zapatistas went through a long internal review and announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas, and moving authority toward a more local level, a Local Autonomous Government in each community, which can coordinate through regional collectives, but making clear that the coordinating levels depend on the communities and aren't above them.

In most institutions, as time goes on, more and more layers and offices are added, but in their review the Zapatistas took the opposite approach and pushed authority downward. And did they publish a book on leadership, and then open a certification program? Nope. They simply changed the system they were actually living in.

Also, I need to restrain my enthusiasm here. This level of autonomy is born out of communities with long histories (Indigenous communities that share language, family ties, long struggles for land, and decades of defending themselves together). So a new ecovillage can't just "copy" the visible diagram and instantly have the trust underneath it.

Additionally, the Zapatistas themselves say that Zapatismo cannot be imported or exported. What can be "imported" is the idea of building and asking questions, and when things don't work, changing the structure so that they will.

This, however, does not prove my point about moving to a model where internal necessities are not purchased, creating a common purse, and eventually eliminating the need for outside money altogether. The Zapatistas do use collective work for many things (schools, clinics, autonomous government, resistance activities, etc.), but also produce things for sale, engage in trade, and receive support from outside. However, what they do show is that it is possible for an entire community to eliminate the need to purchase, on the market, most major necessities and public functions. It may be helpful to bring in outside help to build capacities, but it's important to realize that if that help is indispensable, then the person/organization providing the help becomes a gatekeeper, and an asymmetric power dynamic of dependence is created.

texts.161g-P16e: In the context of this research I have also looked for evidence of the long-term impact of the Escuelita. While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn't find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then setting up a new communal institution, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita, so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn't prove the Escuelita was responsible. Nonetheless I'm borrowing their teaching method and their ambition to replicate, not claiming they already proved my whole model.
texts.161g-P17e2: Sociocracy has a very different history, yet some similar features have emerged there as well: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority with linking between the levels. Does this prove there's a universal formula? No. But it means that people building institutions of this sort have another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.
